draft.title: Building at Deir el-Bahri
card: Deir el-Bahri is a site on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes. Hatshepsut built her mortuary temple there, where offerings would be made to her after death.
The temple was built in terraces, rising in levels against the cliffs. Long ramps and colonnades (rows of columns) joined the levels.
Reliefs are scenes carved into the walls. Hatshepsut's reliefs recorded events of her reign, such as her trading expedition to Punt.
The temple also honoured the god Amun. Its carvings and chapels linked Hatshepsut to him, which supported her right to rule.
draft.remember: The temple was both a place for her afterlife and a public record of her reign and her tie to Amun.

a.q: What was the main purpose of the reliefs in Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri?
opts: To record her achievements and link her to Amun
To mark the border of her kingdom at Thebes
To list the taxes paid to her by the priests
To show the plans used to build the terraces
a.why: The reliefs were carved scenes that told of her reign and showed her bond with Amun. They were not plans or tax records: the temple was built to honour her and the god, not to run the state.
a.clue: Think about what a ruler wanted visitors to see and remember.

b.q: A historian studies a carved wall scene at Deir el-Bahri that shows Hatshepsut's reign. What kind of evidence is it for her reign?
opts: A relief made at her order, showing how she wished to be seen
A neutral report written by a foreign observer at the time
A private letter from one of her officials to a friend
A record made after her death by Thutmose III in anger
b.why: The reliefs were carved during her reign and shaped what she wanted people to believe about her rule. A historian must allow for that purpose. The scenes were not a neutral outsider's report, and they were not made by Thutmose III after her death.
b.clue: Who ordered the temple to be built, and why?
